title: Asking the calculator for help
blurb: The model can use an ordinary calculator, outside the model, for exact sums. In the new design (being built), the talker writes the call as plain text at the end of a turn, the calculator writes back plain text, and the whole reader reads the reply. The results here are from the tested version.

scenes.heading: Why a calculator? Code adds exactly

caption.text: Code adds two numbers exactly, every time.
A learned network has to learn each sum from practice.
In the new design, the talker writes its sum on a text slip (made-up numbers here) and sends it to a calculator outside the model. The whole reader reads the reply.

scenes.heading: Tested version: copying digits with a pointer, a step left, a stop
scenes.question: Tom has 12 apples. (made-up example)

caption.text: In the tested version, to write the 12 in a call, the call writer's learned pointer lands on its last digit, the 2.
The copy then steps one letter left and copies the 1.
A learned stop head says when to stop.

In the tested version, the copy trick was used for 98% of written operands and, by today's stand-in talker, for 91.5% of answers, on all six separate copies (T1SDR). The planned talker and the new design use no pointer or copying.
Copied here means the copy trick was used, not that the copy was right.

scenes.heading: Tested version: the reply goes through the reader into the notes

caption.text: In the tested version, in our made-up Tom example, after round 2 the call writer writes sub 12 5 as text, and the outside calculator replies.
The reply, sub 12 5 = 7, comes back as text. In the tested version the reader's letter window reads it, and it is added to the notes. The new design uses the whole reader, Gemma plus the window.
The question is not read again. After round 3 the call writer writes add 7 3, and the calculator replies 10.
